name: Deliver Results
definition: Leaders focus on the key inputs for their business and deliver them with the right quality and in a timely fashion. Despite setbacks, they rise to the occasion and never settle.
why: Deliver Results is where the rest of the principles get cashed. {lp:ownership}, {lp:customer-obsession}, and {lp:bias-for-action} are why you deliver. {lp:think-big}, {lp:invent-and-simplify}, {lp:dive-deep}, {lp:are-right-a-lot}, {lp:insist-on-the-highest-standards}, and {lp:frugality} decide what is worth delivering. {lp:hire-and-develop-the-best}, {lp:have-backbone-disagree-and-commit}, and {lp:earn-trust} are how the work actually gets through other people.

Look for commitments that landed, not for a tour of the process. This is not a think tank. A clever theory that never ships is a hobby. Leaders push the thing through to the end. They invent around the obstacle. They do not settle for good enough when the customer still feels the gap.

Delivery is not blind activity. It is the right result: the one that helps the customer, hits the date, and does not steal from quality, scale, or the next year. You prioritize. You will trade a lesser goal to protect the one that matters. You will not burn the team to look busy, and you will not treat the date as a nice-to-have.
Setbacks are part of the job. The principle is what you do next. Rise to the occasion. Do not rewrite the goal so the miss looks like a plan.
calibrationIntro: Score whether someone finishes the right work, on time, at the right quality, without burning people or the future. Under misses or settles. Over hits a number by breaking trust, quality, or the team.

rows.under: Misses the mark and ships a good-enough product.
rows.justRight: Hits the date with work that was planned and is actually good.
rows.over: Decides on almost no data and cuts other people out in order to hit the date.

rows.under: Does not put enough time or people on the work, and quality suffers.
rows.justRight: Uses the people on the team well and delivers quality through clear, shared decisions.
rows.over: The result is fine, and it consumed far more resource than the thing was worth.

rows.situation: When tracking whether you are on track
rows.under: Reviews metrics now and then. Accepts excuses for underperformance.
rows.justRight: Reviews the success metrics on a steady cadence and balances the short term with the longer term.
rows.over: Pushes results every day with no sense of the structure underneath. The team exhausts and output falls.

rows.under: Lets the team invent new metrics so often that progress cannot be compared week to week.
rows.justRight: Keeps a stable set, and still asks whether those metrics are the ones that matter.
rows.over: Stares at last week's number and never looks at whether the work will matter next quarter.

rows.situation: When something is in the way
rows.under: Is so understanding of every obstacle that no workaround ever appears.
rows.justRight: Names the obstacles early and either delivers the goal or delivers a workaround that still serves the customer.
rows.over: Gets the result and burns every bridge. Escalates as a habit.

rows.situation: When you cannot hit every goal
rows.under: Misses the objective and has not lined up the work that would finish it if a dependency opened.
rows.justRight: Hits the goals that matter and will trade a lesser one to protect a more important one.
rows.over: Hits most of the list by making poor calls, and misses the one that was actually critical.

rows.under: Loses focus. Is not motivated. The work drifts.
rows.justRight: Stays on the long-term result and sets a pace the team can run again next month.
rows.over: Piles on work that a team can survive for a short burst and then burns out.

rows.situation: When dates are on the calendar
rows.under: Treats dates as optional. Slips have no consequence.
rows.justRight: Sets a realistic schedule and delivers on it.
rows.over: Publishes an unreal schedule to squeeze out more work, then slips anyway.

rows.under: So flexible that nothing is fixed. Scope keeps moving and the team wastes the week.
rows.justRight: Changes the deliverable when the business really changed, and holds still when it did not.
rows.over: Follows the first plan after it has stopped making sense.

rows.situation: When the team has to live through the delivery
rows.under: Does not deliver. Planning is weak, focus is gone, and nobody is motivated.
rows.justRight: Delivers the project and the weekly work with a planned load the team will still accept tomorrow.
rows.over: Delivers by forcing long nights until people start to hate the job.

examples.title: Invent around the blocked path
examples.body: A dependency does not land. The weak move is to wait and then miss. The calibrated move is to name the obstacle early, build the workaround, and still put something useful in the customer's hands on the date. Deliver Results is the invention you do when the original plan dies.

examples.title: Hit the date without stealing from quality
examples.body: The date is real. Cutting the last week of hardening would make the demo look done and the next month look like an outage. The leader cuts scope that the customer will not feel, keeps the hardening, and ships on time. That is the right quality, in a timely fashion. A heroics week is the other failure mode.

examples.title: Trade the lesser goal
examples.body: The annual list has ten items. Two of them move the customer and the business. A new, more important request arrives in May. The leader drops a lesser item on purpose, writes down the trade, and still finishes the two that matter. Finishing eight of the wrong things is not delivery.

looksLike.individual: An individual who delivers can tell you the input they own, the date, the quality bar, and the last obstacle they invented around. Their work is done when the customer can use it, not when the ticket is closed. They do not need a crisis to find another gear, and they do not disappear when the first plan breaks.
looksLike.manager: A manager who delivers keeps a short list of the inputs that matter, reviews them on a cadence, and will trade a lesser goal in public. They set dates the team can believe. They do not accept a theater of excuses, and they do not get the number by burning people or partners. After a setback they raise the energy; they do not rewrite history.

deepen: What result were you on the hook for, and how would a customer have known you delivered it?
Which input actually moves the business, and how much time last week went to something else?
What obstacle did you invent around, and what obstacle did you only empathize with?
If a key person had been out for two weeks, would the date still have held?
Are you measuring a stable set of metrics, or did the scoreboard change whenever the news was bad?
Which goal did you drop on purpose so a more important one could finish?
When the date slipped, did you treat it as a broken promise or as a flexible suggestion?
Who is using what you shipped, and is it behaving the way you said it would?
Did the team still want to work together the Monday after you hit the date?
Where did you settle for good enough while the customer could still feel the gap?

related.note: Speed gets you to the first result. Delivery is finishing the right one.
Owners do not stop at a blocker that sits outside their box.
A result that fails the quality bar is not a result. It is a defect with a ship date.
You cannot manage the key inputs if you do not know what is actually moving them.
Delivery without a larger aim is a busy calendar. The vision still has to ship.
A result that does not help the customer is activity.
What is worth delivering is often the simpler path, not the extra feature.
You cannot deliver the right thing if the call was wrong.
What is worth delivering includes what you refuse to spend.
You do not deliver at scale with a weak team.
The work gets through other people when you will disagree, then commit.
Delivery through other people requires they believe you.
